name: Jayanth
definition: Jayanth is a composite portrait of a Kodava pepper-nursery and homestay owner in his early forties, navigating the coffee and spice economy of Somwarpet taluk with pride in his heritage and anxiety over succession and market swings. He stands at the intersection of Kodagu's traditional plantation life and its newer tourism economy, balancing family land, hired migrant labour, government neglect of compensation and roads, and the question of whether his children will return.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Jayanth owns a fifteen-acre family estate inherited through the patrilineal okka system, planted with coffee, pepper, cardamom and a few areca palms, supplemented by a three-room homestay he and his wife opened in 2017. The coffee harvest runs November through February, when he employs six seasonal workers from Assam and Odisha, paying them around ₹450 per day plus meals and shed housing. Pepper vines climb the silver-oak shade trees, and he maintains a small nursery selling rooted pepper cuttings to neighbouring estates, earning ₹25,000–₹30,000 in a good monsoon year. The homestay brings in another ₹60,000–₹80,000 annually from trekking tourists and Bengaluru families, though bookings dropped sharply during the 2018 floods and again during the pandemic. His wife manages the cooking and laundry; he drives guests to Igguthappa temple or the Abbey Falls viewpoint in his aging Bolero. Income swings with the Coffee Board's post-blossom estimate and the pepper price, which crashed below ₹300/kg in 2023 before recovering slightly. He worries the Kasturirangan notification will freeze any expansion or building, a fear sharpened by the September 2026 all-party resolution he read about in Udayavani but whose legal force he does not trust.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Jayanth lives in the family ainmane, a tile-roofed ancestral home his grandfather built, with his wife Kaveri, his mother, his son Aditya (twenty, studying hotel management in Mysuru), and his daughter Nandini (seventeen, in second PUC at a private college in Madikeri). His father passed away in 2015. Kaveri, also Kodava, married into the okka twenty-two years ago in a traditional wedding without a Brahmin priest, the couple circling the sacred lamp while clan elders blessed them. She keeps the household accounts, manages the homestay bookings via a travel aggregator app, and cooks pandi curry and kadambuttu for guests. Jayanth's mother, now seventy, helps with the kitchen garden and the annual Puthari harvest festival, when the family offers the first rice to the clan deity. Gender roles in the household follow a practical division: Kaveri's labour is recognised but unpaid, while Jayanth holds title to the land and deals with banks and labour contractors. He hopes Aditya will return and take over the estate and homestay, but his son speaks of hotel jobs in Bengaluru or Dubai, and Nandini wants to study nursing in Manipal, mirroring the outmigration trend he sees among cousins and neighbours.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Jayanth studied up to second PUC at the government college in Somwarpet, then dropped out to help his father on the estate when coffee prices were good and labour was cheaper. He regrets not finishing, though he reads Kannada newspapers daily and has taught himself basic bookkeeping and homestay marketing. Aditya attended the Kodava Vidyalaya boarding school in Gonikoppa through Class 10, then moved to a private PU college in Mysuru; fees, hostel and food cost the family around ₹1.2 lakh per year, financed partly by a Canara Bank education loan. Nandini commutes daily to Madikeri, a forty-minute drive on a road that turns treacherous in the monsoon; the family pays ₹35,000 per year in college fees. Both children studied in Kannada medium through Class 10, then switched to English for PU science, a transition Nandini found difficult. Jayanth is proud that both are on track to join professions his father never imagined—hotel management, nursing—but he worries they see the estate as a fallback, not a future. The 2018 floods closed schools for three weeks and damaged the Somwarpet college building; classes resumed in a repaired block, but the memory of that disruption lingers. He wants his children to have choices, yet he knows that if neither returns, the estate may be leased or sold, breaking a lineage his okka has held for four generations.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Jayanth's family relies on the government Primary Health Centre in Somwarpet for fevers and minor injuries, but serious cases mean a two-hour drive to Madikeri's district hospital or, increasingly, to Mysuru's larger hospitals. His mother has diabetes and high blood pressure, managed with monthly doctor visits and daily tablets that cost around ₹800 per month. The estate's location near the Pushpagiri Wildlife Sanctuary means constant vigilance for leptospirosis during the rains—Jayanth ensures workers wear boots in the fields and boils all drinking water. One of his Assamese workers fell sick with high fever and body ache in 2022; the PHC diagnosed leptospirosis and referred him to Madikeri, where he recovered after a week of intravenous antibiotics. Jayanth paid for the hospital stay, knowing that without it the man would have left mid-harvest and word would spread, making future hiring harder. Snakebite is a real risk; a neighbour's daughter was bitten by a pit viper two years ago and reached Madikeri just in time for antivenom. Pesticide exposure from spraying coffee and pepper is a low-level worry—Jayanth has started using organic fungicides after a Coorg Planters' Association workshop, but many neighbours still use cheaper chemical options. The family has health insurance under a private scheme that costs ₹18,000 annually, covering hospitalisation but not outpatient medicines, which add up.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Jayanth's identity is rooted in his Kodava okka, the patrilineal clan that traces its ainmane to this land and links him to cousins across Somwarpet and Virajpet. The okka meets for Puthari, the harvest festival in December, when the family offers new rice and celebrates with pandi curry, and for Kail Podh in September, when the men clean and worship the family's licensed firearms—a tradition Jayanth upholds with pride, though he rarely hunts. He speaks Kodava Takk at home and with clan elders, switching to Kannada for business and with his children, who understand Takk but reply in Kannada or English. The family visits the Igguthappa temple in Kakkabe for major festivals and has taken part in the Kodava Family Hockey Tournament, though Jayanth himself no longer plays. He is aware of the Kodava National Council's language-recognition and autonomy demands and broadly supports them, feeling that Kodagu's distinct culture is misunderstood or dismissed by Bengaluru bureaucrats. Relations with the Tibetan settlement families near Bylakuppe are cordial but distant—some buy coffee from him, and he has hired Tibetan workers in the past. The local Gowda and migrant-labour families live separately; Jayanth employs them but socialises mainly within Kodava circles. He attends Kaveri Sankramana at Bhagamandala when he can, joining the throng that gathers where the river is said to rise.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Jayanth's encounters with government are marked by frustration and mistrust. After an elephant destroyed part of his pepper crop and damaged a shed in 2020, he filed for Forest Department compensation; the claim took eighteen months to process, and he received ₹35,000 against an estimated loss of ₹80,000. The delay and partial payout feed his belief that the state neglects Kodagu's farmer-wildlife conflict while prioritising conservation. The Taluk Panchayat has funded a culvert repair near his estate and a water pipeline extension, but the main Somwarpet-Madikeri road remains pocked with potholes that worsen every monsoon, a standing grievance. Jayanth has heard of Jal Jeevan Mission tap-water schemes but his household has a borewell and does not depend on piped supply. He availed a small NABARD loan in 2015 for drip irrigation, which he repaid on time. The Kasturirangan Western Ghats ESA notification terrifies him; he attended a Coorg Planters' Association meeting in 2024 where the consensus was that the notification would freeze land use and kill livelihoods. The September 2026 all-party resolution gave him brief hope, but he doubts Bengaluru or Delhi will listen. His view of government is transactional: he pays property tax, files GST returns for the homestay, and expects roads, hospitals and fair compensation in return. When those fail, he falls back on the okka and neighbours.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Jayanth is proud to be Kodava and to own land his forebears cleared and planted, yet he is haunted by the possibility that neither of his children will carry it forward. He blames the lack of a railway line in Kodagu, the crumbling roads and the government's indifference to plantation farmers' struggles. The 2018 floods shook him; his family was safe, but friends in Makkandur lost homes, and the relief effort felt slow and chaotic. He worries that another such disaster will come, and that this time the state will be even less prepared. The Kasturirangan notification looms as an existential threat: he imagines officials arriving to tell him he cannot expand his homestay or replant a hillside patch, land his family has held for generations suddenly declared off-limits. He is angry that conservationists in Bengaluru or Delhi, who have never faced an elephant in the dark or lost a season's pepper to disease, can dictate his livelihood. At the same time, he takes quiet pride in Kodagu's forests, wildlife and the coffee heritage that draws tourists from across India. He hopes for a government that will defend farmers' rights, compensate losses promptly and build the roads and railway Kodagu has long deserved, but he has learned not to expect it. His deepest fear is that in twenty years the estate will be silent, sold to an outsider or leased to a corporate operator, the ainmane empty, and the Kodava Takk his mother speaks fading into memory.
